title: Multi-Step Instructions
readingMarkdown:
# Multi-Step Instructions

Most real requests are procedures. "Check this expense claim" means: read it, confirm there is a receipt, compare the amount with the limit, decide, give the reason. A person who has done the job for a year performs those steps without being told. A model has to be told, and how it is told decides whether every step is done.

This chapter is about instructions with several steps inside **one prompt**. Module 5.6 covered the other arrangement, in which each step is its own prompt and code passes results along. Here the model holds the whole procedure and is trusted to walk through it. The chapter explains why models skip and merge steps, how to write a procedure that leaves no room for it, and how to make the model's progress visible so that a skipped step can be seen.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### The recipe and the checklist

Two familiar documents show what good multi-step instructions look like.

A **recipe** written for a beginner numbers its steps and puts one action in each. It gives quantities and times: "simmer for 12 minutes", not "simmer until done". It says what to do at a fork: "if the sauce is too thick, add two spoons of water". And it says when to stop.

A **checklist** is what a pilot reads before take-off. It is not there because pilots do not know how to fly. It is there because a person doing a familiar sequence under pressure will, sooner or later, leave a step out, and will not notice. In 2009 a study in eight hospitals around the world introduced a 19-item checklist to be read aloud at three points during surgery. Deaths fell from 1.5 percent to 0.8 percent, and major complications from 11.0 percent to 7.0 percent. Nothing in the list was new to the surgeons.

A model following a procedure has the weaknesses of both the beginner cook and the experienced surgeon. Like the beginner, it knows only what the page says. Like the surgeon, it can go through a long sequence fluently and omit one item without any sign that it did so.

So a multi-step prompt needs both documents: a recipe to say what to do, and a checklist to confirm it was done.

### What goes wrong, in one picture

```text
   WHAT YOU WROTE                         WHAT THE MODEL DID

   "Read the claim, check the             read the claim
    receipt and the limit, then           checked the receipt
    decide and explain."                  (limit check dropped)
                                          decided
                                          explained, confidently

   WHAT YOU SHOULD HAVE WRITTEN           WHAT YOU GET BACK

   1. Read the claim. Write the           STEP 1: USD 240, hotel
      amount and category.                STEP 2: RECEIPT OK
   2. Receipt present? Write it.          STEP 3: NEEDS APPROVAL
   3. Above the limit? Write it.          STEP 4: Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL
   4. Write the decision.                 STEP 5: Reason: above the limit
   5. Write the reason.                   STEP 6: Checked
   6. Check against the list.
                                          a missing line is a visible gap
```

The second version does two things the first does not. Each step is separate, so none can hide inside another. And each step leaves a line of output, so its absence shows.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### One prompt or several

A procedure can be given to a model in two ways.

| | Steps inside one prompt (this chapter) | One prompt per step (Module 5.6) |
|---|---|---|
| Who keeps track of the steps | The model | Your code |
| Calls to the model | One | One per step |
| Cost and delay | Lower | Higher |
| Can a step be skipped | Yes, and silently unless you make it visible | No: the code runs every step |
| Can each step be checked before the next | Only afterwards | Yes, with a gate |
| Suits | Short procedures, a person in a chat window | Long or high-stakes procedures, automation |

Module 5.6 advised starting with one prompt and splitting only where it fails. This chapter is how to make the one prompt as reliable as it can be, and how to tell when it has reached its limit.

### Why models skip and merge steps

A procedure in a prompt is text that influences what the model writes. It is not a program, and nothing counts through its lines. Seven things follow from that.

**Compound steps.** "Check the receipt and the limit" is one sentence holding two actions. The model does the first, feels the sentence is satisfied, and moves on. This is the commonest cause of a dropped step, and the easiest to fix.

**Steps with no output.** "Consider whether the amount is reasonable" asks for nothing to be written. A step that produces nothing can be omitted with no trace, and the model is under no pressure to perform it.

**Open conditions.** "If the amount is over the limit, flag it" says nothing about the other case. The model must guess whether to say anything, and you cannot tell "checked and fine" from "never checked".

**The pull of the answer.** If the final answer looks obvious from the first two steps, the model tends to go straight to it. A claim with a receipt looks approvable, so the limit check is the one that vanishes.

**Position.** Module 5.3 showed that material in the middle of a long input is used least. In a ten-step procedure the middle steps are the ones at risk.

**Too many instructions.** A 2025 study, "How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once?", gave models up to 500 simple instructions at a time and counted how many were obeyed. Adherence fell steadily as the number rose, and even the best models tested followed only about two thirds of them at 500. No model follows an unlimited list.

**Loops with no bound.** "Keep improving it until it is good" has no test for "good" and no limit. The model either stops after one pass or carries on rewriting.

Research on step-by-step reasoning found the same pattern from the other side. A 2023 paper, "Plan-and-Solve Prompting", examined the mistakes models made when simply told to think step by step, and named missing steps as one of the three main kinds of error, beside calculation errors and misunderstanding the question. Its remedy was to have the model first write out a plan and then carry it out, which reduced the missing steps.

### The parts of an unambiguous procedure

| Part | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | Says what the procedure is for, so that judgement calls go the right way | "Decide whether an expense claim can be paid" |
| **Numbered steps** | Fix the order and let you refer to a step | "3." |
| **One action per step** | Stops one action hiding behind another | "Write the amount and the category" |
| **An output for every step** | Makes the step's completion visible | "Write RECEIPT OK" |
| **Both branches of every condition** | Removes the guess | "If above the limit, write NEEDS APPROVAL. Otherwise write WITHIN LIMIT" |
| **Bounded repetition** | Prevents endless or absent loops | "Revise at most 2 times" |
| **A stop rule** | Says when the work is finished and what not to do beyond it | "Stop after step 6. Do not contact the claimant" |
| **A final check** | Catches what slipped through | "Check the decision against the checklist" |

The fourth row deserves emphasis. When every step always writes something, including "nothing to do here", an absent line can only mean an absent step.

### From vague to exact

| Vague | Exact |
|---|---|
| "Check the receipt and the limit" | Two steps, each with its own output |
| "If it is over the limit, flag it" | "If the amount is above the limit, write NEEDS APPROVAL. Otherwise write WITHIN LIMIT" |
| "Handle anything unusual appropriately" | "If the category is not in the list, write UNKNOWN CATEGORY. Otherwise write CATEGORY OK" |
| "Summarise briefly" | "Summarise in at most 40 words" |
| "Repeat until it is correct" | "Check it against the list. Revise at most 2 times" |
| "Then finish up" | "Stop after step 6" |

The test for a step is whether two careful people, given the same input, would write the same thing. Words such as "appropriately", "relevant", and "as needed" fail it, because they hand the decision back to the reader.

### Thinking step by step, then and now

In 2022 a paper titled "Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners" reported that adding the sentence "Let's think step by step" raised one model's accuracy on a set of arithmetic word problems from 17.7 percent to 78.7 percent. Asking a model to write its reasoning before its answer, known as chain of thought, became a standard technique.

The models have since changed. Current reasoning models work through a problem before answering whether or not they are asked to. A 2025 report from the Wharton School tested the instruction on such models across repeated trials and found gains of only about three percent, at a cost of 20 to 80 percent more time. For models that do not reason by default, the gains were larger on average and came with more variable answers.

Two different things are being asked for, and they should be kept apart.

| | "Think step by step" | "Follow these steps" |
|---|---|---|
| Who chooses the steps | The model | You |
| What it improves | Reasoning on a problem | Compliance with a process |
| Value on current reasoning models | Small | Undiminished |

A model that reasons well still does not know that your company checks the receipt before the limit, or that a decision must name the amount. The procedure is information the model lacks. That is why writing procedures remains necessary when the old incantation is not.

When you do not know the steps yourself, the Plan-and-Solve approach is the useful one: ask the model to write a numbered plan first, read it, correct it, and then tell it to carry the plan out.

### Intermediate outputs

The single most effective defence against skipped steps is to require a line of output per step:

```text
After each step, write one line starting with "STEP n:" followed by the result of that step.
```

These lines do three jobs. They make the model perform the step, because it has to produce a result. They give later steps something definite to use: step 4 can refer to "the result of step 3". And they let a few lines of code confirm that every step was done, in order, once.

They cost output tokens, and the end user rarely wants to see them. Both problems have the same answer: your code reads the markers, checks them, and shows the user only the final line. Module 5.5's structured output is the stricter form of the same idea, with one field per step.

### How long can a procedure be?

Suppose each step is carried out correctly with probability $p$, independently. The probability that all $n$ steps are right is

$$
P(\text{all correct}) = p^{n}
$$

This is the compounding from Module 2.12 and Module 5.6, now inside a single prompt.

| Steps | $p = 0.90$ | $p = 0.95$ | $p = 0.99$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.900 | 0.950 | 0.990 |
| 3 | 0.729 | 0.857 | 0.970 |
| 5 | 0.590 | 0.774 | 0.951 |
| 10 | 0.349 | 0.599 | 0.904 |
| 20 | 0.122 | 0.358 | 0.818 |

At 95 percent per step, a ten-step procedure is followed completely about 60 percent of the time. Turning the formula round gives the longest procedure that meets a target $t$:

$$
n_{\max} = \left\lfloor \frac{\ln t}{\ln p} \right\rfloor
$$

For $p = 0.95$ and a target of 0.8, the ratio is 4.35, so four steps: $0.95^{4} = 0.815$ and $0.95^{5} = 0.774$. For $p = 0.99$ and a target of 0.9, ten steps.

There are two ways to do better than the table. Raise $p$, which is what the rewriting above does. Or detect and repair failures, which is what markers and a final check do: a skipped step that is seen can be asked for again.

### Verification steps and checklists

A final step that checks the work catches some of what the earlier steps got wrong. Three forms are in use.

**A self-check.** "Before you finish, check the answer against this list" is the cheapest. It helps, and it has a limit: the same model that made the mistake is reading its own work, and tends to approve it.

**An independent check.** A 2023 paper, "Chain-of-Verification", had a model draft an answer, write questions that would test the draft's claims, answer those questions separately without looking at the draft, and then revise. Answering separately was the point, since it stopped the draft's errors being repeated. This reduced fabricated facts in the final answers. The evaluator pattern of Module 5.6 is the same idea with a second prompt.

**A check in code.** Whatever can be tested mechanically should be: the decision is one of three allowed words, the reason names an amount, the reply is under the word limit. Code does not get tired and does not approve its own work.

A good checklist is short, and each item is a question with a yes or no answer. "Is the tone right?" is not a checklist item. "Is the reply at most 80 words?" is.

### When to stop adding steps and split

Move from one prompt to a chain when any of these holds: the procedure has more steps than the table above allows for your target; one step needs a tool or a lookup; a mistake at one step is expensive enough that it must be checked before the next begins; or the audit keeps finding the same step missing after you have rewritten it.

### Complexity

Formatting and linting a procedure are linear in its length. Auditing markers is linear in the length of the output. The checklist is linear in the number of checks times the length of the output. The procedure itself adds its own length to every request's input, and the markers add one line per step to the output.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, a linter for the steps and a formatter that turns them into a prompt.

```python
import re

VAGUE = ("appropriately", "properly", "as needed", "relevant", "and so on")
MARKER_LINE = 'After each step, write one line starting with "STEP n:" followed by the result of that step.'

def words_of(text):
    return " " + " ".join(re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", text.lower()).split()) + " "

def lint_procedure(steps):
    problems = []
    for number, step in enumerate(steps, start=1):
        text = words_of(step)
        if " then " in text or ";" in step:
            problems.append((number, "compound"))
        if any(" " + phrase + " " in text for phrase in VAGUE):
            problems.append((number, "vague"))
        if " if " in text and " otherwise " not in text:
            problems.append((number, "open-condition"))
        if (" repeat " in text or " until " in text) and " at most " not in text:
            problems.append((number, "unbounded"))
    return problems

def format_procedure(goal, steps, stop_rule):
    if not steps:
        raise ValueError("a procedure needs at least one step")
    lines = ["Goal: " + goal.strip(), "", "Follow these steps in order. Do not skip or merge steps."]
    lines += [f"{number}. {step.strip()}" for number, step in enumerate(steps, start=1)]
    lines += ["", "Stop rule: " + stop_rule.strip(), "", MARKER_LINE + " Number of steps: " + str(len(steps)) + "."]
    return "\n".join(lines)

BAD_STEPS = [
    "Read the claim and then work out the amount and category",
    "Check the receipt",
    "If the amount is over the limit, flag it",
    "Deal with anything unusual appropriately",
    "Repeat until the claim is correct",
]
GOOD_STEPS = [
    "Read the claim. Write the amount and the category",
    "If there is no receipt, write NO RECEIPT. Otherwise write RECEIPT OK",
    "If the amount is above the limit for its category, write NEEDS APPROVAL. Otherwise write WITHIN LIMIT",
    "If step 2 gave NO RECEIPT, write Decision: REJECT. Otherwise write Decision: APPROVE or Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL to match step 3",
    "Write Reason: and one sentence that names the amount",
    "Check the decision and the reason against the checklist. Revise at most 2 times",
]
print(lint_procedure(BAD_STEPS))
print(lint_procedure(GOOD_STEPS))
print(format_procedure("Decide whether an expense claim can be paid.", GOOD_STEPS,
                       "Stop after step 6. Do not contact the claimant."))
```

- **`words_of` reduces a step to lowercase words with a space at each end.** Searching for a word with a space on both sides matches it only as a whole word, so "then" is not found inside "authentic".
- **Four faults are detected, each from Section 2.** The word "then" or a semicolon marks a step holding two actions. A word from `VAGUE` hands a decision back to the reader. An "if" with no "otherwise" leaves one branch unstated. A "repeat" or "until" with no "at most" is a loop without a bound.
- **The bad procedure has four findings.** Step 1 is compound, step 3 has an open condition, step 4 is vague, and step 5 is unbounded.
- **Step 2 of the bad procedure passes, and is still bad.** "Check the receipt" does not say what to write. A linter that looks for words cannot see a missing output. It finds the cheap mistakes and leaves the rest to a reader.
- **The good procedure has no findings.** Each condition states both branches, the one repetition is bounded, and every step says what to write.
- **`format_procedure` adds what the steps cannot say for themselves.** It states the goal, numbers the steps, forbids skipping and merging, gives the stop rule, and asks for a marker line per step. It also states the number of steps, so the model knows how many markers are expected.

Next, auditing the markers in what the model wrote.

```python
def audit_markers(output, total):
    seen = [int(number) for number in re.findall(r"(?m)^STEP (\d+):", output)]
    return {
        "missing": [number for number in range(1, total + 1) if number not in seen],
        "repeated": sorted({number for number in seen if seen.count(number) > 1}),
        "in_order": seen == sorted(seen),
    }

MODEL_OUTPUT = """STEP 1: USD 240, hotel
STEP 2: RECEIPT OK
STEP 4: Decision: APPROVE
STEP 5: Reason: the claim is for a hotel stay of USD 240.
STEP 6: Checked."""
print(audit_markers(MODEL_OUTPUT, 6))
print(audit_markers("STEP 2: b\nSTEP 1: a\nSTEP 2: c\nNote that STEP 3: is not at the start of a line", 3))
```

- **The pattern finds markers at the start of a line only.** A mention of "STEP 3:" in the middle of a sentence is not a marker, and is not counted.
- **Three things are reported.** The steps with no marker, the steps with more than one, and whether the markers appear in ascending order.
- **The model's output is missing step 3.** That is the limit check. The model saw a receipt, went straight to a decision, and approved a claim of USD 240 against a limit it never looked up. The decision reads perfectly well. Only the gap in the numbering reveals the fault.
- **The second example has every kind of fault.** Step 3 is missing, step 2 appears twice, and the order is wrong.
- **The audit proves presence, not correctness.** A marker shows that the model wrote something for the step. Whether what it wrote is right is a matter for the final check.
- **What to do with a gap.** Send one follow-up naming the missing step, or run the request again. If the same step is missing repeatedly, rewrite that step, or move it into its own prompt.

Then, how long a procedure can be.

```python
def max_steps(p, target):
    count = 0
    while count < 1000 and p ** (count + 1) >= target:
        count += 1
    return count

for p in (0.90, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(p, [round(p ** n, 3) for n in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20)], max_steps(p, 0.8), max_steps(p, 0.9))
```

- **The loop counts steps while the product stays at or above the target.** It is the formula from Section 2, computed by multiplication, which avoids taking the logarithm of awkward values.
- **The cap of 1,000 keeps the loop finite.** A value of `p` equal to 1 would otherwise never fall below any target.
- **The output is the table from Section 2 with two more columns.** At 0.90 per step, a target of 0.8 allows two steps and a target of 0.9 allows one. At 0.95 the answers are four and two. At 0.99 they are 22 and ten.
- **Small gains per step are large gains overall.** Moving from 0.95 to 0.99 per step raises the allowable length for a 0.9 target from two steps to ten. That is the return on rewriting a vague step.

Finally, a checklist for the finished answer.

```python
def run_checklist(output, checks):
    failed = []
    for name, kind, value in checks:
        if kind == "contains":
            passed = value.lower() in output.lower()
        elif kind == "not_contains":
            passed = value.lower() not in output.lower()
        elif kind == "max_words":
            passed = len(output.split()) <= value
        elif kind == "matches":
            passed = re.search(value, output) is not None
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown kind of check: " + kind)
        if not passed:
            failed.append(name)
    return failed

CHECKS = [
    ("states an allowed decision", "matches", r"Decision: (APPROVE|NEEDS APPROVAL|REJECT)"),
    ("gives a reason", "contains", "reason:"),
    ("names the amount", "matches", r"USD \d+"),
    ("makes no promise of payment", "not_contains", "will be paid"),
    ("is at most 30 words", "max_words", 30),
]
print(run_checklist("Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL. Reason: the hotel claim of USD 240 is above the USD 200 limit.", CHECKS))
print(run_checklist("Approved, looks fine to me. It will be paid on Friday.", CHECKS))
```

- **Each check is a name, a kind, and a value.** The name is what a person reads in the report. The kind selects one of four tests, and the value is what it tests for.
- **Every check has a yes or no answer.** There is no item asking whether the answer is "good". Each one can be decided by a line of code.
- **The function returns the names of the failed checks.** An empty list is a pass. A list of names tells the model, or a person, exactly what to fix.
- **The first answer passes all five.** The second fails four: it states no allowed decision, gives no labelled reason, names no amount, and promises payment. It is short enough.
- **An unknown kind is an error.** A misspelt kind that silently passed would be a check that never ran.

**Complexity.** `lint_procedure` and `format_procedure` are linear in the text of the steps. `audit_markers` is linear in the output. `max_steps` takes at most 1,000 multiplications. `run_checklist` is linear in the number of checks times the length of the output.

### A procedure template

```text
Goal: [what this procedure decides or produces, in one sentence]

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip or merge steps.
1. [One action. Say what to write.]
2. If [condition], write [A]. Otherwise write [B].
3. [One action, using the result of step 2.]
4. Check the result against the checklist below. Revise at most 2 times.

Checklist:
- [A question with a yes or no answer]
- [A question with a yes or no answer]

Stop rule: Stop after step 4. Do not [anything outside the task].

After each step, write one line starting with "STEP n:" followed by the result of that step.
```

### Reviewing a procedure before you use it

| Question | If the answer is no |
|---|---|
| Does each step hold exactly one action? | Split it |
| Does each step say what to write? | Add an output |
| Does every "if" have an "otherwise"? | Add the other branch |
| Is every repetition bounded? | Add "at most N times" |
| Would two people write the same thing for each step? | Replace the vague word with a number, a list, or a test |
| Is there a stop rule? | Add one |
| Is the number of steps within what your target allows? | Shorten it, or chain it |

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**The paragraph procedure.** Steps written as running prose, joined with "and", "then", and "after that", are the form most likely to lose a step. Numbering them is the largest improvement for the least effort.

**"And" inside a numbered step.** People number their steps and leave two actions in step 3. The linter in this chapter looks for "then" and semicolons. "And" is harder to detect, because it also joins harmless pairs such as "the amount and the category". Read each step and ask whether it produces one result or two.

**The silent branch.** "If there is a problem, report it" leaves the model to decide whether "no problem" deserves a line. Always state both branches. The habit feels pedantic and removes a whole class of ambiguity.

**No marker, no proof.** A reply that reads well tells you nothing about whether step 3 was done. Without a line of output per step you are trusting the model's fluency. Ask for the markers, and check them in code.

**Markers shown to the customer.** The step lines are working notes. Parse them, keep them in your logs, and show the user only the final result.

**A marker written without the work.** Sometimes a model writes "STEP 3: done" and does nothing. Ask for the result, not a confirmation: "write the limit you found and the amount", not "confirm you checked the limit".

**"Think step by step" as a cure-all.** On current reasoning models the phrase adds little and costs time. It also does not tell the model which steps your process needs. Write the steps.

**Self-checks that approve everything.** "Check your work" as a last step is weak, because a model reviewing its own answer usually agrees with it. Give it a specific list to check against, or check in code, or use a separate prompt.

**The ever-growing procedure.** Every incident adds a step. After a year there are 25, the middle ones are routinely skipped, and nobody knows which still matter. The arithmetic of Section 2 applies: past a handful of steps, split the procedure into a chain with checks between the parts.

**Conflicting steps.** Step 2 says to be brief and step 7 asks for a full explanation. The model obeys whichever it met last, or whichever is more forcefully worded. Read the procedure end to end for contradictions, as Module 5.7 advised for the rules in a system prompt.

**Order that does not match the work.** Steps listed in the order the author thought of them, not the order they must be done in, invite the model to follow the page. If step 5 needs the result of step 6, renumber.

**Unbounded revision.** "Improve it until it is perfect" gives a model no way to know when to stop. Give a test and a limit: "revise at most 2 times, and stop as soon as every item on the checklist passes".

**Testing on one input.** A procedure that works on the example in front of you may skip a step on a different kind of input. Run it on a varied set and count how often each step's marker is missing. The step that goes missing most is the one to rewrite.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** A multi-step instruction is a procedure that the model, not your code, must walk through. Because a prompt is text and not a program, steps can be skipped or merged without any sign: compound steps lose their second action, steps with no output leave no trace, open conditions hide whether a check was made, and middle steps of long lists are followed least. An unambiguous procedure has a goal, numbered steps with one action each, an output for every step, both branches of every condition, bounded repetition, a stop rule, and a final check. Requiring a marker line per step turns an invisible omission into a visible gap that a few lines of code can detect. Asking a model to think step by step matters little on current reasoning models, while telling it which steps to follow matters as much as ever. If each step is right with probability $p$, all $n$ are right with probability $p^{n}$, which limits how long a single-prompt procedure can usefully be and is the signal for moving to a chain.

**Question 1.** A procedure has 12 steps, and each is carried out correctly 98 percent of the time, independently. What is the probability that all 12 are carried out correctly? What is the longest procedure that keeps this probability at or above 0.9? The team proposes splitting the 12 steps into three prompts of four steps each. Does splitting change the probability by itself, and what does it make possible?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The probability that all 12 steps are right is 0.98 to the power 12, which is about 0.785. So more than one run in five has at least one faulty step, although each step taken alone looks very reliable. For a target of 0.9, the longest procedure is the largest n with 0.98 to the power n at or above 0.9. The natural logarithm of 0.9 is about minus 0.1054, and of 0.98 about minus 0.0202, and their ratio is about 5.2, so five steps: 0.98 to the power 5 is about 0.904, and to the power 6 about 0.886. Splitting into three prompts of four steps does not change the arithmetic by itself. Each prompt succeeds with probability 0.98 to the power 4, about 0.922, and all three succeed together with probability 0.98 to the power 12 again, the same 0.785. Twelve steps are twelve steps however they are grouped. What splitting makes possible is a check between the parts. With one prompt, the model carries a fault from step 3 through nine more steps before anyone can look. With three prompts, code can inspect the result of each part, with a marker audit and a checklist, and repeat that part alone if it fails. It is the checking and repeating, not the splitting, that raises the overall figure, which is the lesson of the gates in Module 5.6.

</details>

**Question 2.** Rewrite this instruction as an unambiguous procedure and explain each change: "Look at the customer's review and work out what they are unhappy about, then if it is a delivery problem apologise, and write a reply that deals with their concerns appropriately, improving it until it sounds right."

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

One sound rewriting has five steps. Step 1: read the review, and write the main complaint in at most 15 words. Step 2: if the complaint is about delivery, write DELIVERY, and otherwise write OTHER. Step 3: if step 2 gave DELIVERY, write one sentence of apology for the delay, and otherwise write NO APOLOGY. Step 4: write a reply of at most 80 words that answers the complaint from step 1 and includes the sentence from step 3 if there is one. Step 5: check the reply against the checklist, revise at most 2 times, and stop. The checklist would ask whether the reply mentions the complaint, whether it is at most 80 words, and whether it avoids promising a refund. A stop rule and a request for a marker line per step complete it. The changes are these. The original is one sentence holding four actions joined by "and" and "then", so it is split into numbered steps with one action each, which stops the later actions being dropped. "Work out what they are unhappy about" produced nothing, so step 1 now writes the complaint, which makes the step visible and gives later steps something to use. The condition "if it is a delivery problem apologise" said nothing about other problems, so both branches are stated, and a missing apology can be told apart from a skipped check. "Appropriately" handed the judgement back to the model, so it is replaced with what the reply must contain and a word limit. "Until it sounds right" had no test and no bound, so it becomes a check against a list with at most two revisions.

</details>

**Question 3.** A five-step procedure asks for a marker line per step. The model's output contains, in this order, lines beginning "STEP 1:", "STEP 2:", "STEP 2:", and "STEP 4:". State what an audit reports. Then explain what the audit cannot tell you, and what you would do next.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The audit reports that steps 3 and 5 are missing, that step 2 is repeated, and that the markers are in ascending order, since the sequence 1, 2, 2, 4 never goes backwards. So two of the five steps left no trace, and one step was written twice, which often means the model merged step 3 into a second attempt at step 2 or restarted partway. The audit cannot tell you whether the steps that are present were done correctly. A marker proves that a line was written for a step, not that the line is right, and a model can write a plausible result without doing the work. It also cannot tell you why the steps are missing. Next, look at what step 3 and step 5 ask for. If step 5 is the final check, its absence means the answer went out unverified, so the answer should not be used as it stands. Send a follow-up asking for steps 3 and 5 by number, or rerun the request, and run the checklist in code on the final answer whatever the markers say. Then find out whether this was a one-off: run the procedure on a varied set of inputs and count how often each marker is missing. If step 3 is often missing, rewrite it, checking for a compound action, an open condition, or no stated output. If it is still skipped, move it into its own prompt so that code, and not the model, guarantees it runs.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: Write, Lint, and Audit a Procedure
interactiveLab.context: A finance team wants an assistant to check expense claims by following the same six steps every time, and has found that the assistant sometimes skips the limit check. You will build a formatter for a numbered procedure, a linter for ambiguous steps, an audit of the step markers in a model's output, a calculator for how long a procedure can safely be, and a final checklist.

    print("audit    :", audit_markers(MODEL_OUTPUT, 6))

steps.title: Format a numbered procedure
steps.instruction: Implement format_procedure(goal, steps, stop_rule). If steps is empty, raise ValueError. Build a list of lines: 'Goal: ' followed by the stripped goal; a blank line; the sentence 'Follow these steps in order. Do not skip or merge steps.'; one line per step numbered from 1 in the form '1. step text', with each step stripped; a blank line; 'Stop rule: ' followed by the stripped stop rule; a blank line; and finally MARKER_LINE followed by ' Number of steps: ', the number of steps, and a full stop. Join the lines with newlines. This is the frame from Section 2: a goal, numbered steps, a stop rule, and a visible result for every step. [MOD-5.8]
steps.hintConceptual: A recipe has a title, numbered steps, and a line saying when the dish is done. The steps cannot say for themselves that none may be skipped, so the lines around them say it.
steps.testAssertion:
_text = format_procedure("G", ["a", "b"], "S")
_expected = 'Goal: G\n\nFollow these steps in order. Do not skip or merge steps.\n1. a\n2. b\n\nStop rule: S\n\nAfter each step, write one line starting with "STEP n:" followed by the result of that step. Number of steps: 2.'
assert _text == _expected, f"The procedure has a goal, numbered steps, a stop rule, and the marker line, got {_text!r}"
assert format_procedure("  G  ", ["  a  "], "  S  ") == _expected.replace("1. a\n2. b", "1. a").replace("steps: 2.", "steps: 1."), "The goal, each step, and the stop rule are stripped"
_six = format_procedure("Decide whether an expense claim can be paid.", GOOD_STEPS, "Stop after step 6.")
assert _six.splitlines()[0] == "Goal: Decide whether an expense claim can be paid.", "The goal comes first"
assert _six.splitlines()[3] == "1. " + GOOD_STEPS[0] and _six.splitlines()[8] == "6. " + GOOD_STEPS[5], "Steps are numbered from 1 in order"
assert _six.endswith(MARKER_LINE + " Number of steps: 6."), "The last line asks for a marker per step and states how many steps there are"
assert _six.count("\n") == 12 and "Stop rule: Stop after step 6." in _six.splitlines(), "There are 13 lines, and the stop rule has a line to itself"
def _refuses_empty():
    try:
        format_procedure("G", [], "S")
    except ValueError:
        return True
    return False
assert _refuses_empty(), "A procedure with no steps raises ValueError"
print("Step 1 passed: the procedure has a goal, numbered steps, a stop rule, and a marker for every step.")

steps.title: Lint the steps for ambiguity
steps.instruction: Implement lint_procedure(steps). For each step, numbered from 1, compute text = words_of(step) and report problems in this order. Report 'compound' if ' then ' is in text or a semicolon is in the original step: the step holds two actions. Report 'vague' if any phrase from VAGUE appears in text with a space on each side. Report 'open-condition' if ' if ' is in text and ' otherwise ' is not: one branch is unstated. Report 'unbounded' if ' repeat ' or ' until ' is in text and ' at most ' is not. Return a list of (step number, problem) tuples. Run it on BAD_STEPS and GOOD_STEPS. These are the faults listed in Section 2. [MOD-5.8]
steps.hintConceptual: Read each step as a stranger would. Does it ask for two things at once? Does it use a word that means 'you decide'? Does it say what to do in one case and nothing about the other? Does it say to keep going without saying for how long?
steps.testAssertion:
assert lint_procedure(BAD_STEPS) == [(1, "compound"), (3, "open-condition"), (4, "vague"), (5, "unbounded")], f"The bad procedure has four findings, got {lint_procedure(BAD_STEPS)}"
assert lint_procedure(GOOD_STEPS) == [], f"The good procedure has no findings, got {lint_procedure(GOOD_STEPS)}"
assert lint_procedure(["Do A; do B"]) == [(1, "compound")], "A semicolon marks a compound step"
assert lint_procedure(["Read it THEN sum it"]) == [(1, "compound")], "The comparison ignores case"
assert lint_procedure(["If x, write A. Otherwise write B", "Repeat the check at most 3 times"]) == [], "A condition with both branches and a bounded loop are fine"
assert lint_procedure(["Keep editing until it reads well"]) == [(1, "unbounded")], "'until' with no 'at most' is unbounded"
assert lint_procedure(["Summarise the relevant parts, then stop if done"]) == [(1, "compound"), (1, "vague"), (1, "open-condition")], "One step can have several problems, reported in the stated order"
assert lint_procedure(["Strengthen the motif", "Notify the authentic user"]) == [], "Whole words only: 'then' inside 'Strengthen' and 'if' inside 'motif' do not count"
assert lint_procedure(["Tidy up as needed"]) == [(1, "vague")], "A vague phrase of two words is found"
assert lint_procedure([]) == [], "No steps, no findings"
print("Step 2 passed: compound steps, vague words, open conditions, and unbounded loops are reported.")

steps.title: Audit the step markers
steps.instruction: Implement audit_markers(output, total). Find every marker in the output: a line that begins with 'STEP ', then a number, then a colon. The pattern r"(?m)^STEP (\d+):" with re.findall returns the numbers as strings, in the order they appear; convert them to integers. Return a dict with three keys. 'missing' is the list of step numbers from 1 to total that have no marker, in ascending order. 'repeated' is the sorted list of step numbers that have more than one marker. 'in_order' is True if the markers appear in ascending order, which is the case when the list of numbers equals its sorted self. Run it on MODEL_OUTPUT with a total of 6 and find the step the model skipped. This is the audit from Section 2. [MOD-5.8]
steps.hintConceptual: A register is taken by calling each name and listening for an answer. Silence for a name is an absence. An answer given twice, or out of turn, is also worth noting.
steps.testAssertion:
assert audit_markers(MODEL_OUTPUT, 6) == {"missing": [3], "repeated": [], "in_order": True}, f"The model skipped step 3, the limit check, got {audit_markers(MODEL_OUTPUT, 6)}"
assert audit_markers("STEP 1: a
STEP 2: b
STEP 3: c", 3) == {"missing": [], "repeated": [], "in_order": True}, "A complete output has nothing missing"
assert audit_markers("STEP 2: b
STEP 1: a
STEP 2: c
Note that STEP 3: is not at the start of a line", 3) == {"missing": [3], "repeated": [2], "in_order": False}, "A marker must start a line, and repeats and disorder are reported"
assert audit_markers("STEP 1: a
STEP 2: b
STEP 2: c
STEP 4: d", 5) == {"missing": [3, 5], "repeated": [2], "in_order": True}, "1, 2, 2, 4 of five: steps 3 and 5 are missing, step 2 is repeated, and the order is ascending"
assert audit_markers("", 3) == {"missing": [1, 2, 3], "repeated": [], "in_order": True}, "An empty output is missing every step"
assert audit_markers("The answer is APPROVE.", 2) == {"missing": [1, 2], "repeated": [], "in_order": True}, "A fluent answer with no markers proves nothing"
assert audit_markers("STEP 10: j
STEP 2: b", 10)["in_order"] is False and audit_markers("STEP 2: b
STEP 10: j", 10)["in_order"] is True, "Markers are compared as numbers, so 10 comes after 2"
assert audit_markers("step 1: a
STEP 2 b
 STEP 3: c", 3)["missing"] == [1, 2, 3], "A marker is the exact form: STEP, a number, and a colon, at the very start of a line"
print("Step 3 passed: a skipped step shows up as a gap in the markers.")

steps.title: How long can a procedure be?
steps.instruction: Implement max_steps(p, target). If each step is carried out correctly with probability p, all n steps are correct with probability p to the power n. Return the largest n for which that is at or above target. Start a count at 0, and while the count is below 1000 and p to the power (count + 1) is at or above target, add 1. Return the count. Try a per-step rate of 0.95 with a target of 0.8, then 0.99 with a target of 0.9. This is the formula from Section 2, and it tells you when one prompt should become a chain. [MOD-5.8]
steps.hintConceptual: Each extra step multiplies the chance of a clean run by a number below one. Keep adding steps while the product is still acceptable, and stop at the last one that is.
steps.hintSyntax:
count = 0
while count < 1000 and p ** (count + 1) >= target:
    count += 1
return count
steps.testAssertion:
assert max_steps(0.95, 0.8) == 4, f"At 0.95 per step, four steps keep the rate at or above 0.8, got {max_steps(0.95, 0.8)}"
assert max_steps(0.99, 0.9) == 10, "At 0.99 per step, ten steps keep the rate at or above 0.9"
assert max_steps(0.9, 0.8) == 2 and max_steps(0.9, 0.9) == 1, "At 0.9 per step the limits are two steps and one step"
assert max_steps(0.95, 0.9) == 2 and max_steps(0.99, 0.8) == 22, "At 0.95 for 0.9 the limit is two, and at 0.99 for 0.8 it is 22"
assert max_steps(0.98, 0.9) == 5, "At 0.98 per step, five steps keep the rate at or above 0.9"
assert max_steps(0.9, 0.95) == 0, "If one step already falls below the target, the answer is 0"
assert max_steps(1.0, 0.9) == 1000, "A perfect step never falls below the target, so the cap of 1000 applies"
assert 0.95 ** max_steps(0.95, 0.8) >= 0.8 > 0.95 ** (max_steps(0.95, 0.8) + 1), "The result is the last n that meets the target"
print("Step 4 passed: at 0.95 per step, a procedure longer than four steps falls below 0.8.")

steps.title: Run a final checklist
steps.instruction: Implement run_checklist(output, checks). Each check is a tuple of a name, a kind, and a value. Go through the checks in order and decide whether each passes. A 'contains' check passes if the value appears in the output, ignoring case. A 'not_contains' check passes if the value does not appear, ignoring case. A 'max_words' check passes if the output has at most that many whitespace-separated words. A 'matches' check passes if re.search(value, output) finds a match. Any other kind raises ValueError. Return the list of names of the checks that failed. An empty list means the output passed. Run CHECKS on a good decision and on a careless one. This is the checklist from Section 2: every item has a yes or no answer that code can decide. [MOD-5.8]
steps.hintConceptual: A pilot's checklist has no item that says 'is everything fine?'. Each line is something that is either set or not set. Go down the list and write down the lines that are not.
steps.testAssertion:
_good = "Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL. Reason: the hotel claim of USD 240 is above the USD 200 limit."
_careless = "Approved, looks fine to me. It will be paid on Friday."
assert run_checklist(_good, CHECKS) == [], f"The good decision passes every check, got {run_checklist(_good, CHECKS)}"
assert run_checklist(_careless, CHECKS) == ["states an allowed decision", "gives a reason", "names the amount", "makes no promise of payment"], f"The careless decision fails four checks, got {run_checklist(_careless, CHECKS)}"
assert run_checklist("REASON: x", [("r", "contains", "reason:")]) == [] and run_checklist("It WILL BE PAID", [("p", "not_contains", "will be paid")]) == ["p"], "contains and not_contains ignore case"
assert run_checklist("one two three", [("w", "max_words", 3)]) == [] and run_checklist("one two three four", [("w", "max_words", 3)]) == ["w"], "max_words passes at the limit and fails above it"
assert run_checklist("Decision: MAYBE", [("d", "matches", r"Decision: (APPROVE|REJECT)")]) == ["d"], "matches uses a regular expression"
assert run_checklist(_good + " " + "word " * 30, CHECKS) == ["is at most 30 words"], "An answer that is too long fails only the length check"
assert run_checklist("anything", []) == [], "No checks, no failures"
def _rejects_unknown():
    try:
        run_checklist("x", [("typo", "contians", "x")])
    except ValueError:
        return True
    return False
assert _rejects_unknown(), "A misspelt kind raises ValueError, so that a check can never silently pass"
print("Step 5 passed: the checklist names exactly what a careless answer got wrong.")

interactiveLab.solutionCode:
"""
Lab solution: Write, Lint, and Audit a Procedure
Standard library only.
"""
import re

VAGUE = ("appropriately", "properly", "as needed", "relevant", "and so on")
MARKER_LINE = 'After each step, write one line starting with "STEP n:" followed by the result of that step.'

BAD_STEPS = [
    "Read the claim and then work out the amount and category",
    "Check the receipt",
    "If the amount is over the limit, flag it",
    "Deal with anything unusual appropriately",
    "Repeat until the claim is correct",
]

GOOD_STEPS = [
    "Read the claim. Write the amount and the category",
    "If there is no receipt, write NO RECEIPT. Otherwise write RECEIPT OK",
    "If the amount is above the limit for its category, write NEEDS APPROVAL. Otherwise write WITHIN LIMIT",
    "If step 2 gave NO RECEIPT, write Decision: REJECT. Otherwise write Decision: APPROVE or Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL to match step 3",
    "Write Reason: and one sentence that names the amount",
    "Check the decision and the reason against the checklist. Revise at most 2 times",
]

MODEL_OUTPUT = """STEP 1: USD 240, hotel
STEP 2: RECEIPT OK
STEP 4: Decision: APPROVE
STEP 5: Reason: the claim is for a hotel stay of USD 240.
STEP 6: Checked."""

CHECKS = [
    ("states an allowed decision", "matches", r"Decision: (APPROVE|NEEDS APPROVAL|REJECT)"),
    ("gives a reason", "contains", "reason:"),
    ("names the amount", "matches", r"USD \d+"),
    ("makes no promise of payment", "not_contains", "will be paid"),
    ("is at most 30 words", "max_words", 30),
]


def words_of(text):
    """Provided helper: the text as lowercase words, with one space at each end.
    Searching for " word " in the result matches whole words only."""
    return " " + " ".join(re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", text.lower()).split()) + " "


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def format_procedure(goal, steps, stop_rule):
    """The steps cannot say for themselves that they must all be done, in order, with a
    visible result each. The frame around them says it."""
    if not steps:
        raise ValueError("a procedure needs at least one step")
    lines = ["Goal: " + goal.strip(), "", "Follow these steps in order. Do not skip or merge steps."]
    lines += [f"{number}. {step.strip()}" for number, step in enumerate(steps, start=1)]
    lines += ["", "Stop rule: " + stop_rule.strip(), "", MARKER_LINE + " Number of steps: " + str(len(steps)) + "."]
    return "\n".join(lines)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def lint_procedure(steps):
    """Finds the cheap mistakes: two actions in a step, a vague word, a condition with one
    branch, a loop with no bound. It cannot see a step that fails to say what to write."""
    problems = []
    for number, step in enumerate(steps, start=1):
        text = words_of(step)
        if " then " in text or ";" in step:
            problems.append((number, "compound"))
        if any(" " + phrase + " " in text for phrase in VAGUE):
            problems.append((number, "vague"))
        if " if " in text and " otherwise " not in text:
            problems.append((number, "open-condition"))
        if (" repeat " in text or " until " in text) and " at most " not in text:
            problems.append((number, "unbounded"))
    return problems


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def audit_markers(output, total):
    """A marker proves that something was written for a step. It turns a silent omission
    into a visible gap. It does not prove that what was written is right."""
    seen = [int(number) for number in re.findall(r"(?m)^STEP (\d+):", output)]
    return {
        "missing": [number for number in range(1, total + 1) if number not in seen],
        "repeated": sorted({number for number in seen if seen.count(number) > 1}),
        "in_order": seen == sorted(seen),
    }


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def max_steps(p, target):
    """If each step is right with probability p, all n are right with probability p ** n.
    This is how long a single-prompt procedure can be before a chain is the better design."""
    count = 0
    while count < 1000 and p ** (count + 1) >= target:
        count += 1
    return count


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def run_checklist(output, checks):
    """Every item has a yes or no answer that code can decide. The failed names tell the
    model, or a person, exactly what to fix."""
    failed = []
    for name, kind, value in checks:
        if kind == "contains":
            passed = value.lower() in output.lower()
        elif kind == "not_contains":
            passed = value.lower() not in output.lower()
        elif kind == "max_words":
            passed = len(output.split()) <= value
        elif kind == "matches":
            passed = re.search(value, output) is not None
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown kind of check: " + kind)
        if not passed:
            failed.append(name)
    return failed


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(lint_procedure(BAD_STEPS))
    print(lint_procedure(GOOD_STEPS))
    print(format_procedure("Decide whether an expense claim can be paid.", GOOD_STEPS,
                           "Stop after step 6. Do not contact the claimant."))

    print(audit_markers(MODEL_OUTPUT, 6))
    print(audit_markers("STEP 2: b\nSTEP 1: a\nSTEP 2: c\nNote that STEP 3: is not at the start of a line", 3))
    print(audit_markers("STEP 1: a\nSTEP 2: b\nSTEP 2: c\nSTEP 4: d", 5))

    for p in (0.90, 0.95, 0.99):
        print(p, [round(p ** n, 3) for n in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20)], max_steps(p, 0.8), max_steps(p, 0.9))
    print(round(0.98 ** 12, 3), max_steps(0.98, 0.9), round(0.98 ** 5, 3), round(0.98 ** 6, 3), round(0.98 ** 4, 3))

    print(run_checklist("Decision: NEEDS APPROVAL. Reason: the hotel claim of USD 240 is above the USD 200 limit.", CHECKS))
    print(run_checklist("Approved, looks fine to me. It will be paid on Friday.", CHECKS))
